title: Why Rejoin UNIDO? Reforms, Results, and the Case for a Seat at the Table
label: 15 Sep 2026 · UNIDO evidence
summary: The International Agreements Committee questioned three UNIDO directors about why the UK should rejoin the organisation after withdrawing in 2012. The witnesses described sweeping management reforms, tripled funding mobilisation and doubled technical delivery; pointed to UK-supported projects on steel and cement decarbonisation, hydrogen in Namibia and agri-tech in Ghana; and argued that UK taxpayers get better oversight and influence inside the governing bodies than as a non-member donor. Members pushed back repeatedly on whether joining adds value beyond project funding and whether reforms will outlast the current leadership.

chapters.title: Reforms since the UK left
chapters.takeaway: UNIDO says it has restructured its management, tripled funding and doubled project delivery since the UK withdrew.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: What's actually changed since the UK pulled out? What have you fixed that was a problem back then?

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: The UK's decision was fair and rational. It was never about our mandate—it was about how efficiently we ran the place. So that's where we've worked hardest.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: The current Director-General came in four years ago from a German ministerial job with a very private-sector mindset. He did two rounds of restructuring, brought in outside business consultants, and cut a whole layer of management—without firing anyone, just not replacing people who retired.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: In four years we've tripled our funding mobilisation. The UK is now our second-largest donor. We've also doubled what we actually deliver on the ground—around £400 million this year, up from roughly £190 million.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: The UK gave us an £80 million test project to see if the reforms were real. It went well, so it grew to about £140 million. That trust was earned, not assumed.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: We've also opened up to the private sector in a way that's unusual for a UN agency. That means companies get a foot in markets they couldn't easily reach, and there's a clear business case, not just charity.

chapters.title: Energy access and what Members see on the ground
chapters.takeaway: Members push back that energy investment still isn't reaching the poorest countries, while UNIDO argues energy must be tied to industrial demand.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: I travel across developing countries constantly. Large parts of the DRC still have no electricity at all. I don't see private or public investment actually landing where it's needed. Where is your money really going, and how do you measure it?

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: You're right that only a handful of countries attract investment right now. Least developed countries and small island states still get far too little.

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: We host forums to push for redirection of financial flows, and nationally we help countries build industrial transformation investment plans. Energy isn't just about lighting—it's the backbone, and industry is the engine that turns it into jobs.

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: For example, we're working with west Africa, under Sierra Leone's presidency, on economic corridors and mineral beneficiation. That shifts the conversation from just energy access to energy as an industrial opportunity.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: But communities live off small businesses, and those can't grow without any power at all. Sometimes you need to start where growth can actually happen, with local people, not just the macro picture.

chapters.title: Fitting into UN reform and avoiding duplication
chapters.takeaway: UNIDO says it's part of the wider UN80 reform, focusing on who does what best and outsourcing back-office functions to other agencies.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: All UN agencies are under severe financial pressure. What is UNIDO doing to support the Secretary-General's reform effort to cut staff and programmes?

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: Because of the UK's withdrawal and others before it, we'd already been forced to reform before the current UN80 exercise. So we were somewhat ahead of the shock.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: The first job in the UN80 working groups was being honest about who's good at what. Our mandate is industrial development under SDG 9, and we should be clear where we overlap with UNDP or FAO.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: The most interesting part is back-office functions. Why do our own HR and procurement when agencies like UNOPS or WFP are faster? We're looking at what to outsource rather than duplicate.

turns.speaker: Jason Slater
turns.text: A practical example: we partnered with UNOOSA, the space agency, on Space4Industry. Industrial development depends on connectivity and geospatial data, so jointly we can deliver early-warning systems to protect industrial zones from climate risk.

chapters.title: UK money at work: concrete projects
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses cite UK-funded work on steel and cement carbon standards, a Brazil partnership, hydrogen in Namibia and agri-tech in Ghana.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Can you give us two or three concrete examples of what UK money actually delivered on the ground?

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: First, we're working on global standards for carbon accounting in steel and cement, using UK expertise and industry knowledge. That matters for global trade.

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: Second, we're linking UK and Brazilian innovation ecosystems on steel and cement decarbonisation—UK universities and SMEs helping Brazil build its industrial decarbonisation roadmap.

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: Third, through the Accelerate-to-Demonstrate Facility, we're supporting Namibia's first hydrogen production programme, and biogasification in Kenya's tea industry. These are UK technology and know-how applied in developing countries.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: UK taxpayers have spent decades on food security and linking farmers to markets. What practical examples do you have, maybe with FAO? If not, please write to us—we need to show what difference the money makes.

chapters.title: The rice project and food security
chapters.takeaway: A Ghana rice project cut post-harvest losses from 20% to 13% in six months, though Members stress agronomists are just as vital as technology.

turns.speaker: Jason Slater
turns.text: In Ghana, about 50% of rice is imported, and we found around 20% of domestic production was lost post-harvest. We built a tool the farmer holds in their hand—they scan the rice and trace where losses occur.

turns.speaker: Jason Slater
turns.text: Within six months losses dropped from 20% to 13%. It was funded by Japan, not the UK, and we're now looking to replicate it across west Africa.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Alongside the technology, agronomists are the greatest asset a community has—they know the soil better than anyone. You could eliminate much of the loss by making sure they're in the mix.

chapters.title: Why join rather than just fund projects?
chapters.takeaway: UNIDO argues the UK already pays in but has no seat or vote, so formal membership buys accountability, influence and access, not just project delivery.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We have a huge development office already. What are you doing that we can't do ourselves? Why do we need to rejoin rather than just fund projects?

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: Japan is giving us about £200 million for Ukraine's recovery. Italy funds coffee value chains, and companies like Illy and Lavazza rely on our certification to prove sustainability to consumers.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: The harder point is political. You're already one of our biggest contributors, but you're not formally a stakeholder. You can't vote in the Industrial Development Board, and you don't get due diligence over how the money is spent.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: If the membership fee is small compared to your voluntary contributions and can be found within existing resources, joining is almost a no-brainer. You get a voice, oversight and accountability.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: I don't see any good reason to join except a talking shop. Money isn't reaching villages that need electricity. Why is that better value than funding projects we already trust?

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: I've seen it personally—solar mini-grids in Chad, small hydropower in Madagascar, vocational training for ex-combatants in west Africa. That work is tangible.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: What we were missing was scale. The average project used to be £2 million; with private sector involvement it can now be £200 million. That changes the impact entirely.

turns.speaker: Jason Slater
turns.text: On Ukraine, FCDO and Innovate Ukraine came to us because we have on-the-ground co-ordinators they don't have. Together with Japan and Austria, we can scale what they couldn't do alone.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Isn't that evidence we'd be better off funding projects we have a mutual interest in and seeing the results?

turns.speaker: Jason Slater
turns.text: No, because of what happens after the project ends. We set up a finance coalition at London Climate Action Week to leverage private financing and amplify impact beyond any single project.

chapters.title: Scale, leadership and the long term
chapters.takeaway: Members warn about the failure to scale globally; UNIDO points to leadership development, new financing tools and embedding private sector partnerships as the answer.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: The whole development sector has failed to scale. We'll miss the SDGs otherwise. We need practical examples of scaling up to be convinced.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: You say it's better to be inside. Convince the sceptics here that we're not just buying into bureaucracy.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: It sounds like the Director-General has done a great job, but what happens when he retires? It could revert. This is a long-term commitment—weave that into your answers.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: You should be part of the growth story. Beyond projects, we need UK know-how on industrial policy research, business innovation and reforming our IT and results systems. Other member states won't allow those contracts unless you're a member.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: Other UN agencies now come to us to learn about business innovation, which never used to happen. Being part of that trend ensures it continues, politically and technically.

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: On scaling energy: rural demand is low, so industry has to be the anchor load that makes the business case. We're preparing countries for concessional finance and private capital, not just development finance.

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: And you build institutions through people. The Director-General has invested in leadership training across the organisation, so there's a deep bench to carry this beyond his term.

turns.speaker: Jason Slater
turns.text: I've been through several DFID assessments and seen the shift. It's about implementation modalities—knowing what we're good at, building consortia, and developing new financial instruments like a transformation fund.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all—that's been hugely helpful. We're grateful you travelled from Vienna and wish you a safe journey home.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Please keep supporting Lavazza.
